terms.definition: This category covers the basic rights that tenants have, their ability to organize or unionize, their ability to participate in the housing market or government agencies, and other related issues. This includes how a tenant in public or subsidized housing has rights to participate in decisions about the housing quality and modernization. It also covers rights around raising grievances and advocating for themselves.

terms.name: Landlord access to a rental
terms.definition: This category covers issues a tenant might have with how and when the landlord can access their rental home, and how they have 'quiet enjoyment' to their home. This covers private rentals, subsidized rentals, and public housing. It includes issues of landlords coming onto the property too frequently, unnecessarily, or without proper notice.

terms.name: Leases and Rental Agreements for a rental home
terms.definition: This category covers the process of receiving, understanding, negotiating, and signing a lease between a landlord and tenant. This includes how a tenant can ensure the lease is fair, raise any objections, protect their rights, and deal with other issues with the lease. It can also be about how to understand, modify, or challenge a lease after signing it.

terms.name: Local regulations of rental housing
terms.definition: This category covers state, city, and other local rules that control how property-owners can rent out homes.

terms.name: Problems with paying rent
terms.definition: This category covers situations where the tenant is unable to pay their rent in full and on time.

terms.name: Ending a rental lease early
terms.definition: This category covers situations in which a landlord or tenant wants to end a rental agreement early, in order to have the tenant leave before the lease specifies. This could be in situations where the tenant is unhappy with the housing, and wants to leave early. Or it could be when the landlord wants to have the tenant leave, even though the lease is for a longer term.

terms.name: Landlord pursuing tenant for money owed
terms.definition: This category covers situations when a landlord brings a lawsuit against present or past tenants, to recover money from them. This could include attempts to recover rent that was not paid, penalties, fees, or other financial damages that the landlord believes they have suffered. This could be filed alongside an eviction lawsuit, or separate from it.

terms.name: Retrieving Abandoned Personal Property in a Rental Home
terms.definition: This category covers what happens to a person's property (like furniture, electronics, and other possessions) in their rental home, if they are evicted or leave the home. It covers topics like how long a person has to retrieve their property, how to take care of it, and how to deal with law enforcement or the landlord, roommates, or others if there is a conflict about the property.

terms.name: Renters' housing issues after a natural disaster
terms.definition: This category covers issues a renter might have with their housing after a natural disaster like a flood, hurricane, tornado, or other problem. This includes damage to their home, landlords' responsibility for repairs, eviction, and other issues.

terms.name: Having pets or assistance animals in a rental home
terms.definition: This category covers a renter's options about having a pet in their rental home. This includes rights to have a pet, like for a disability, common lease clauses about pets, what the landlord is able to do, what common problems occur, and more.

terms.name: Utilities - Energy and Heating at home
terms.definition: This category is about electric, energy, gas, and water utilities at home, including financial assistance, utilities being shut off, payment to them, or terminating them. It might also include issues if a utility company is in a crisis, and you must pay another party (like a receiver) instead of the company.

terms.name: Utility disconnection and reconnection
terms.definition: This category covers what might happen if a utility service disconnects for one's home, like for nonpayment of bills. It can cover what notification requirements exist, how to reconnect the services, and getting payment plans.

terms.name: Challenging utility bills
terms.definition: Legal issues related to disputing utility bills that appear unusually high, incorrect, or inaccurate. This includes questions about billing errors, meter problems, estimated charges, rate application, and a customer’s rights to review, dispute, or correct utility charges. This issue covers situations where a person believes their electricity, gas, water, sewer, trash, or other utility bill does not reflect actual usage or lawful rates. Problems may arise from faulty meters, estimated readings, billing mistakes, leaks, incorrect account information, or sudden rate changes. Legal questions often involve how to request an explanation, obtain usage records, ask for a meter test, or file a formal dispute with the utility provider or regulator. It also includes understanding protections against shutoff while a bill is being disputed, options for payment plans or credits, and remedies if the utility fails to correct an error. Rules and procedures vary by utility type (public or private), service provider, and jurisdiction, and may include oversight by public utility commissions or local agencies. Includes: - Disputing unusually high or unexpected utility bills - Billing errors, estimated charges, or meter inaccuracies - Requests for usage records or meter testing - Utility dispute and complaint procedures - Protections against shutoff during a billing dispute - Credits, adjustments, or payment plans related to disputed charges

terms.name: Foreclosure on a Home
terms.definition: This category is about problems with homes you own or live in, that are going into foreclosure, how to defend against it, and the court process around it.

terms.name: Defenses against a Foreclosure
terms.definition: This category concerns options a homeowner may have to defend against a foreclosure action. These defenses can include that the bank didn't follow state procedures; that the loan holder can't prove that they own the loan (they lack standing); that the mortgage servicer make a serious mistake; that the homeowner is a service-member on active duty; or that the statute of limitations has passed.

terms.name: Stopping a foreclosure through a 'redemption' (paying off loan in full)
terms.definition: This category covers the option for a homeowner to 'redeem' their property within a certain time period in a foreclosure process, by paying off their debt or reimbursing the person who bought the property at the foreclosure sale. The options vary by state, about whether this redemption period is only before a foreclosure sale, or after the sale as well.

terms.name: Stopping a foreclosure by reinstating (catching up with) the loan
terms.definition: This category covers options for a homeowner who wants to stop a foreclosure, by 'reinstating' their loan through paying back money they owe (but not the full loan), and then keep up their monthly payments and other fees. States may have different deadlines for when reinstatement may occur, and different lenders may have different policies on reinstating the loan. This category covers how you can use reinstatement as a defense against foreclosure, and also contesting an incorrect reinstatement quote from the lender.

terms.name: Tenant options when landlord is in foreclosure or bankruptcy
terms.definition: This category covers what a tenant can do when their landlord's property is in foreclosure, or if their landlord is in the bankruptcy process. It covers what their rights are, what happens if they face eviction based on their landlord's situation, how their lease may change, or if there are new owners of the property.

terms.name: Owning a Home
terms.definition: This category concerns issues for homeowners, like with improvements, contractors, neighbors, mortgages, taxes, and titles. It also includes problems with owning a home, including foreclosures and liens. It includes scenarios like being the target of misleading or dishonest mortgage lending practices, being told by a lender that extra financial products needed to be purchased to get a mortgage, falling several payments behind on a mortgage or having a home going into foreclosure, and having trouble selling or buying property.

terms.name: Liens on a Home
terms.definition: This category concerns liens taken out on one's home. When borrowing money to pay for a home, one can use a lien to have the property serve as collateral. If one fails to meet payments or other requirements, the lien allows the lender to foreclose on the home and take the property. This might include mortgage liens.

terms.name: Title to a home
terms.definition: This category concerns how to have a 'Title' to one's home, to show that one owns a home. This includes issues on how couples can arrange for multiple people to have 'title' to a home, how to change title to a home, or how to clear title one's home. This also includes issues around title when buying or selling a home, like needs to clear title to home, do title searches, get title insurance, and other issues.

terms.name: Zoning and Land Use of property
terms.definition: This category covers issues a property owner might have with dealing with local government, to get approvals for what they might do with their property. It might include issues around dealing with government's zoning designations, redevelopment or additions, environmental issues, selling or acquiring properties, or other issues.

terms.name: Property Taxes
terms.definition: This category covers issues that a homeowner might have around paying their taxes for their property. This category covers how the taxes are calculated, how to pay them, and how to deal with disputes around them.

terms.name: Mortgages and other financing for a home
terms.definition: This category covers issues that a homeowner might have with taking out a mortgage, finding support and opportunities, dealing with scams, keeping up on their obligations, and understanding their options if problems arise.

terms.name: Dividing (Partition) a home with another owner
terms.definition: This category covers options for when there are multiple property owners, how to divide the land or home with the other people. This might be with a sibling, friend, partner, or spouse. This covers options the person has to go to court for a 'partition' to officially divide their ownership rights and the property with an agreement they all live by.

terms.name: Property disputes with neighbors
terms.definition: Legal issues related to disputes between neighboring property owners or occupants about boundaries, use, access, or control of property. This includes disagreements over where property lines are, what each person is allowed to do on or near the property, and whether a neighbor has improperly used, occupied, or altered someone else’s property. This issue covers situations where a neighbor places items on another person’s property, installs structures or fixtures without permission, encroaches across a boundary, or claims rights that are disputed. Common problems include fences, trees, driveways, shared walls, easements, utility lines, sheds, cameras, or other installations that affect property use or ownership. Disputes may arise because of unclear boundaries, informal agreements, long-standing use, or lack of documentation. It also includes understanding legal rights and remedies related to property boundaries and neighbor conduct, such as requesting removal of encroachments, clarifying boundary lines, asserting ownership or access rights, and resolving conflicts through communication, mediation, or legal action. Legal questions may involve deeds, surveys, easements, local ordinances, and property law principles. Outcomes and procedures vary by jurisdiction and the type of property involved. Includes: - Boundary or property line disputes - Neighbor encroachment or unauthorized use of property - Disputes over fences, structures, or installations - Claims about easements, access, or shared areas - Neighbors placing belongings on another person’s property - Conflicts over rights to use or control property

terms.name: Selling one's home
terms.definition: Legal issues related to selling residential real estate, including understanding ownership rights, disclosure obligations, title requirements, contracts, and closing procedures. This includes both voluntary sales and court-ordered sales. This issue covers situations where a homeowner wants to sell their property and needs to understand the legal steps involved. Questions often arise about confirming ownership, resolving title issues, disclosing known defects, complying with local and state laws, and reviewing purchase agreements. Sellers must typically ensure that the title is clear, liens are addressed, and required disclosures are provided to buyers. It also includes complications such as co-ownership disputes, divorce or probate involvement, outstanding mortgages or tax liens, homeowner association rules, tenant-occupied properties, and capital gains tax considerations. Legal questions may involve negotiating contracts, handling contingencies, responding to inspection issues, and ensuring proper transfer of title at closing. Requirements and risks vary by jurisdiction and by the specific circumstances of the sale. Includes: - Preparing property for sale and confirming ownership - Required seller disclosures - Reviewing and negotiating purchase agreements - Clearing liens or title defects - Coordinating with real estate agents and escrow - Selling jointly owned or court-involved property - Tax implications of selling a home

terms.name: Eminent domain and condemnation
terms.definition: Government taking of private property for public use, including fair compensation disputes.

terms.name: Real property litigation
terms.definition: Lawsuits involving boundary disputes, title disputes, partition actions, and quiet title.

terms.name: Agricultural land and farmland disputes
terms.definition: Legal issues specific to agricultural real property including farmland ownership and water rights.

terms.name: Environmental contamination of property
terms.definition: Legal issues when property is affected by environmental contamination, mold, or pollution.

terms.name: Housing after a Disaster
terms.definition: This category concerns issues a person might have with their housing after a natural disaster or other emergency. It can include issues around owning, clearing title, rebuilding, and insuring a home when you have experienced or at risk of a disaster. It also includes landlord-tenant and eviction issues.

terms.name: Eviction issues during a public health emergency
terms.definition: This category concerns issues that renters and landlords may face during a public health emergency, including dealing with special protections like eviction moratoriums, non-enforcement of eviction writs, and delayed rent. It also concerns what issues may happen in the immediate wake of the state of emergency, including options for financial assistance, mediation, special courts, or other programs to address possible displacement.

terms.name: Mortgage delinquency and foreclosure prevention after a disaster
terms.definition: This category covers options a homeowner has when they fall behind on mortgage payments because of a natural disaster like a hurricane, flood, wildfire, or earthquake. It includes how to request forbearance from a mortgage servicer (a temporary pause or reduction in payments), what federal disaster forbearance programs exist for loans backed by agencies like FHA, VA, Fannie Mae, or Freddie Mac, and what deadlines apply for requesting this relief. It also covers loss mitigation options available after forbearance ends, like loan modifications that extend the repayment term, reduce the interest rate, or add missed payments to the end of the loan. This category covers how to communicate with a servicer during and after a disaster, what documentation is needed, what protections exist against foreclosure while a loss mitigation application is pending, and how to spot mortgage rescue scams that target disaster-affected homeowners. It also covers what to do if a servicer moves forward with foreclosure despite a pending request for help.

terms.name: FEMA Housing Assistance
terms.definition: This category covers how to apply for housing assistance from FEMA after a natural disaster. It covers who is eligible, what is needed to prove eligibility, and what kinds of assistance you can get to cover the cost of rent, home repairs, or access to government-provided housing.

terms.name: Housing issues after contact with police
terms.definition: This category is about issues people experience with housing options and rights after they have been in the criminal justice system (like after an arrest, incarceration, or other police encounter).

terms.name: Zoning issues related to housing
terms.definition: About questions, regulations, and other concerns about zoning, and what kind of changes or buildings can be made based on zoning rules.

terms.name: Homelessness and Housing Insecurity
terms.definition: This category covers issues, rights, protections, and services for people who are experiencing housing instability or homelessness.

terms.name: Mobile Homes
terms.definition: This category covers issues with owning or renting a mobile home, or living in a mobile home park.

terms.name: Owning a mobile home
terms.definition: This category covers legal issues that a mobile homeowner might have, when their mobile home is in a mobile home park, or on private land.

terms.name: Renting in a Mobile Home Park
terms.definition: This category covers rights and options that tenants of a mobile home might have, in a mobile home park. This also includes special rules around eviction or other problems.

terms.name: Immigration
terms.definition: This category covers visas, asylum, green cards, citizenship, migrant work and benefits, and other issues faced by people who are not full citizens in the US. Scenarios in this category include filling out or filing paperwork relating to U.S. immigration issues and attending any legal actions or proceedings related to U.S. immigration issues.

terms.name: Deportation or Removal of immigrants
terms.definition: This category covers situations in which an immigrant to the United States might be deported or removed, for a criminal situation, or another kind of violation. It also covers waivers and protections against removal, as well as the types of process and immigrant can use to stop the deportation.

terms.name: Criminal conviction leading to deportation
terms.definition: This category covers if and how a criminal conviction can lead to an immigrant's removal from the United States. It covers the process by which a conviction can lead to deportation, and how a person can appeal or stop the deportation.

terms.name: Stopping deportation through Withholding of Removal
terms.definition: This category covers protections a person might have against being deported, particularly if their life or freedom would be threatened in the other country, on account of a protected ground, like race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or otherwise. This could be called 'withholding of removal' or 'non-refoulment'. This category covers how a person can try to use this process to stop their deportation or removal, and how the government will make a decision about it.

terms.name: Waivers of Inadmissibility; Deportation; or Removal
terms.definition: This category covers options for an immigrant to get a waiver from deportation or removal proceedings, or from decisions that they are inadmissible to the US. This waiver may provide them exceptions from the usual rules of deportability or inadmissibility

terms.name: Detention of immigrants
terms.definition: This category covers detention of immigrants in the United States, including how and when a person can be detained, how they might be released on bond, how they might be paroled, and the process and hearings that surround detention.

terms.name: Bond Hearing for a detained immigrant
terms.definition: This category covers the options for an immigrant who is being held in detention in the United States, to be released from detention through a bond hearing. This includes how to request a bond hearing, how the hearing will proceed, and what possible outcomes will result. It also covers the process of paying the bond and having this amount returned.

terms.name: Parole for immigrants
terms.definition: This category covers options for parole, for immigrants who are detained in the U.S. This is about how an immigrant can request parole, in order to be able to leave detention for a temporary period while their case is pending in immigration court. It coves who is eligible, what documents and evidence are needed, and what the terms of the parole will be.

terms.name: Public Benefits for immigrants
terms.definition: This category concerns what public benefit programs an immigrant to the US might be able to access. This includes eligibility and procedural requirements for immigrants for programs like food stamps (SNAP benefits), Medicaid, Medicare, disability, old age, SSI, TANF, welfare, and other assistance programs from the government.

terms.name: Immigration consequences of applying for or using public benefits
terms.definition: This category covers concerns an immigrant may have about whether applying for or receiving public benefits like Medicaid (or Medi-Cal), SNAP, housing assistance, or other government programs will negatively affect their immigration case. This includes how the "public charge" rule works, which benefits are counted in a public charge determination and which are not, and how the rule applies differently depending on a person's immigration status and the type of benefit. It covers what risks exist when applying for a green card, renewing a visa, or adjusting status after using benefits. It also covers situations when a person avoids benefits out of fear even though using them would not affect their case, and how to get accurate information about these rules. This category includes how sponsor "deeming" rules (where a sponsor's income is counted) interact with benefit eligibility, and what obligations a sponsor's affidavit of support creates.

terms.name: Immigrants' access to health care
terms.definition: This category covers issues that immigrants to the US might have when trying to access health care, including programs that cover the costs of care like Medicaid, Medicare, or CHIP.

terms.name: Options for immigration status; visas; permits; and travel papers
terms.definition: This category covers the various status options that an immigrant to the US might have, to enter or to remain in the US. This can include visas, green cards, permits, papers, and other types of legal status.

terms.name: Deferred Action immigration status
terms.definition: This category covers options for an immigrant to get a Deferred Action status, that gives people who are in the US illegally an indefinite delay of their deportation. Deferred Action does not give an immigrant legal status

terms.name: Legalization of undocumented immigrant
terms.definition: This category covers options for an undocumented immigrant in the United States to get a legal status that lets them stay legally. This could be for an immigrant who has entered the country illegally, or one who has overstayed another visa. This includes options for Dreamers, or people who are on the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program. It also includes asylum, U Visas, and other options for people in special situations.

terms.name: Political asylum
terms.definition: This category covers options for an immigrant to apply for political asylum in the United States, including the procedure they must follow, what types of situations are covered, what kind of status are possible as an outcome, and consequences for one's family or a future ability to travel.

terms.name: Immigrants' rights
terms.definition: This category concerns rights that immigrants to the country may have, including around work, standards of treatment, consular notification, and other protections. It also considers limits on the rights of non-citizens, as compared to citizens.

terms.name: Discrimination against Immigrants
terms.definition: This category covers what rights and protections an immigrant might have if they face discrimination at work, at school, in the business, with the government, or otherwise.

terms.name: Sponsoring an immigrant
terms.definition: This category is about options for an individual, a company, or other groups to sponsor an immigrant to the United States, so that they are able to get legal status. This includes both the categories and the process of being a sponsor. It also includes obligations and rules that sponsors must follow.

terms.name: Sponsoring an immigrant for a work visa
terms.definition: This category covers options and procedure for a company or nonprofit that is considering sponsoring a work visa for immigrants to the United States. This covers what different work visas are, the process of being a sponsor, and what obligations and rules the sponsor must follow.

terms.name: Border searches
terms.definition: This category covers problems and rights for a person who is facing a search of their person or their property while crossing a border.

terms.name: Refugees
terms.definition: This category covers options, services, and outcomes for refugees coming from other countries to the United States. This includes who qualifies to enter the country, what visas or options are open to them, what evidence they must prove to get status, and what ongoing services or pathways are open to refugees. This includes asylum options in the US.

terms.name: Going to immigration interviews and hearings
terms.definition: This category is about the process and rights for an immigrant who is going to an administrative hearing, interview, or other kind of official meeting regarding their immigration status and related concerns. It includes their rights to have counsel, how they will be able to participate, what kind of evidence or testimony they my present, and other options and protections they might have. It also includes their obligations and rules about going through this process.

terms.name: Undocumented immigrants
terms.definition: This category covers what options and rights a person may have when in the US as an immigrant without legal stauts.

terms.name: Immigrants working when undocumented or without authorization
terms.definition: This category covers rights and consequences of an immigrant in the US working, without legal status that allows them to work.

terms.name: Immigration options for victims of domestic violence
terms.definition: This category concerns options that non-citizens in the US might have if they are facing domestic violence or abuse, including immigration pathways and other protections.

terms.name: Green Card options for victims of domestic abuse
terms.definition: This category concerns how a spouse or a child of a US citizen might be eligible to apply for Legal Permanent Resident status (LPR, or green card), based on the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA). VAWA also provides that a spouse or child can apply for a 'battered spouse or child waiver' that lets the person with conditional LPR status (often when the marriage is less than 2 years old) -- continue with their LPR status without the other spouse's support. It also includes U-Visa options, with green card options for victims of crimes (including domestic violence).

terms.name: Canceling Removal Proceedings for domestic abuse victims
terms.definition: This category concerns options for a spouse or child of a US citizen or a US Legal Permanent Resident (green-card holder) -- to end the removal proceedings against them. This involves protections under the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA), that allow the spouse or child who is currently in removal proceedings before an immigration judge, to stop these proceedings and to begin an application for legal permanent residency (green card).

terms.name: Migrant and seasonal worker employment
terms.definition: This category concerns issues that migrant and seasonal workers (often working in agriculture) face around employment. It includes situations in which people are working on farms or other agricultural settings, getting permission to work in the US, addressing issues around being undocumented, dealing with sexual violence at work, or seeking protection and employment rights.

terms.name: Work as an immigrant
terms.definition: This category covers options, rights, and rules for immigrants in the U.S. who want to work. This includes how to get authorization to work, the visa statuses that allow work, and rules and penalties for violating rules around work.

terms.name: Getting a work permit as an immigrant
terms.definition: This legal issue covers problems related to applying for, renewing, or maintaining authorization to work in the United States as an immigrant or noncitizen. It includes understanding who is eligible for a work permit (employment authorization), how to apply, what documents are required, and how work authorization is connected to a person’s immigration status or pending immigration case. This category also includes issues involving delays, denials, expirations, or errors related to work permits. People may face problems if their application is incomplete, processing times are long, their status changes, or their work authorization expires before renewal is approved. Legal questions often arise about whether a person can work while an application is pending, how to correct mistakes, or what to do if an employer questions or refuses to accept valid work authorization. In addition, this issue covers the consequences of working without authorization or losing work authorization, including risks to immigration status, employment rights, and income stability. It may involve navigating different types of work permits, eligibility based on specific immigration categories, and understanding protections against employer misuse or discrimination related to work authorization. Includes: Applying for an initial work permit Renewing or replacing a work permit Delays or denials of employment authorization Work authorization while an immigration case is pending Employer issues related to work authorization documents Excludes:

terms.name: Workplace problems for immigrant workers
terms.definition: This category covers situations when an undocumented immigrant is having problems at work, in part because of their status. This could include not being paid fairly by an employer, and feeling unable to complain because of their immigration status. This includes being paid below minimum wage, not receiving overtime, having wages withheld, or being threatened with deportation for raising pay concerns. It covers what rights undocumented workers have to recover unpaid wages (regardless of immigration status), how to file a wage claim without exposing one's status, what labor agency protections exist, and whether cooperating with a labor investigation may qualify a worker for immigration relief. It also covers situations when employers use a worker's lack of documents as leverage to avoid paying what is owed.

terms.name: International family law
terms.definition: Cross-border family law including Hague Convention child abduction and international custody disputes.

terms.name: Money; Debt; and Consumer Issues
terms.definition: This category covers issues people face regarding money, insurance, consumer goods and contracts, taxes, and small claims about quality of service. Scenarios in this category include getting credit because of identity theft, being the target of unfair lending practices or internet scams, problems with debt reduction or credit repair services, problems with terms for repayment of payday lenders, problems related to legal financial obligations, harassment by creditors, problems with pay for or repossession of a car, filing for bankruptcy, garnished wages, and disconnected utilities due to nonpayment or a billing dispute

terms.name: Banking and financial services
terms.definition: Legal issues related to using banks, credit unions, and other financial institutions, including problems with accounts, transactions, fees, loans, credit cards, promotions, errors, fraud, and disputes with financial service providers. This category covers disputes and problems involving checking and savings accounts, credit cards, balance transfers, loans, electronic payments, overdrafts, interest charges, and other financial products or services. Issues may involve billing or processing errors, unauthorized charges, misapplied payments, misleading promotions, account freezes or closures, and failures by financial institutions to follow agreed terms or consumer protection laws.

terms.name: Bank Billing Errors or Unauthorized Charges
terms.definition: This legal issue covers problems where a bank, credit union, or financial institution incorrectly charges interest, fees, or amounts to an account, or processes transactions that the account holder did not authorize. This includes errors in how payments, deposits, balance transfers, or promotional terms are applied, as well as charges that appear without the customer’s consent. This category also includes disputes involving misapplied payments, incorrect interest calculations, duplicate charges, improper overdraft or service fees, and failures to honor advertised or agreed terms. Errors may result from system problems, employee mistakes, or incorrect account coding, and can cause balances to increase unexpectedly or accounts to show inaccurate information. In addition, this issue covers situations where unauthorized transactions occur due to fraud, identity theft, or account compromise, as well as cases where a bank delays or fails to correct known errors after being notified. Legal considerations may include timelines for reporting errors, required investigations by the bank, documentation of disputes, and consumer protection lawsifhts under federal or state law.

terms.name: Paying for medical care
terms.definition: This category covers issues that a person might have to pay for their health and medical care, including through insurance programs, dealing with bills, dealing with medical debt, and other concerns.

terms.name: Health Insurance
terms.definition: This category concerns issues a person might have with getting, using, or maintaining health insurance to pay for medical care. This is primarily about private health insurance (not those provided by government).

terms.name: Free and Low-Cost medical care
terms.definition: This category covers options and services that provide people with free care, or low-cost care.

terms.name: Managed Care plans
terms.definition: This category covers options for a person on a managed care plan, in which a health insurance plan coordinates with providers. This might be through a private provider or a Medicaid program.

terms.name: Debt collection for medical costs
terms.definition: This category covers situations in which a person faces debt collection for medical or dental bills, including calls, letters, warnings, and lawsuits.

terms.name: Contracts; Warranties; and Deceptive Trade Practices
terms.definition: This category concerns issues that consumers and businesses have, including around forming a contract, possible fraud or misrepresentation, payment plans and loans, poor performance, or other problems with the contracting.

terms.name: Corporate and Commercial Contracts
terms.definition: This category concerns contracts that are made between businesses or other entities (not personal/individual ones).

terms.name: Consumer Contract issues
terms.definition: This category concerns problems a consumer might have with a contract they have signed with a business or other entity.

terms.name: Warranty issues
terms.definition: This category concerns problems a consumer might have around a warranty for a product they have purchased. This may be a written warranty a company issues, spoken warranties from a salesperson, service contract warranties, or implied warranties created by state law. This category covers issues with understanding warranty offers, making claims around them, resolving disputes around warranties, or possible lawsuits around enforcing warranties.

terms.name: Credit practices and Credit reports
terms.definition: This category is about the problems a person might have with the information on their credit report, as well as opportunities to clean, mask, expunge, and otherwise remove damaging credit information.

terms.name: Building good credit
terms.definition: This category is about strategies and options a person can use to build credit that can help them access more lending opportunities and other resources.

terms.name: Repairing credit
terms.definition: This category is about how a person can improve their credit and credit report if they have problems they need to address.

terms.name: Finding and understanding a credit report
terms.definition: This category covers how a person can find, understand, and deal with their credit report.

terms.name: Accessing credit and borrowing money
terms.definition: This category covers issues that consumers may have in borrowing money and accessing credit. This could be regarding 'credit invisibles' (consumers who do not have credit records or scores).

terms.name: Fixing errors on a credit report
terms.definition: This category covers how a person can address errors they find on their credit report, where there are mistakes about their finances or other situations.

terms.name: Financial Literacy
terms.definition: This category concerns resources and options for improving a person's ability to understand their finances, and make choices in their best interest.

terms.name: Using Bank Accounts
terms.definition: This category covers issues a person might have in getting and maintaining a bank account. This can be around understanding the options and rules of using banks, and how to maintain a bank account.

terms.name: Using Checks
terms.definition: This category covers issues around a person using checks for their finances, including how to write them, how they work, and what might go wrong.

terms.name: Using Debit Cards
terms.definition: This category covers how a person can use debit cards for their finances, including how to get a card, what fees and penalties there might be, and how the card transactions and payments work.

terms.name: Using Credit Cards
terms.definition: This category covers consumers' issues with getting and using credit cards, or other forms of credit. This includes literacy around how credit works, what consequences there are, and how to maintain and use their credit card.

terms.name: Identity Theft and Lost Credit Cards
terms.definition: This category covers the problems related to having one's identity stolen, or losing sensitive financial information, including the loss of credit cards or government documents.

terms.name: Financial Identity Theft
terms.definition: This category covers problems when a person's information is used by another person to make purchases, get credit cards, rent a home, or get utilities. It also might be for stealing tax refunds, or using checks from the bank account.

terms.name: Criminal Identity Theft with police
terms.definition: This issue concerns what a person can do if their identity has been stolen by a person after they have committed a crime, and have presented themselves to the police with a false identity.

terms.name: Insurance
terms.definition: This category covers consumers' options and rights when getting insurance to protect themselves against accidents, illness, financial demands, and catastrophes. This includes insurance for health, cars, natural disasters, death, homes, and disability.

terms.name: Disputing a denied insurance claim
terms.definition: This category covers what a person can do when an insurance company denies a claim or pays less than expected. This includes how to understand the denial letter and the reason given, how to file an internal appeal with the insurance company, and when and how to escalate to a state insurance department or regulatory agency. It covers common reasons claims are denied, like lapsed coverage, policy exclusions, missed deadlines, or disputes about fault or the value of damages. It also covers situations when an insurance company delays payment unreasonably, acts in "bad faith" by refusing to pay a valid claim, or offers a settlement amount that does not cover the actual loss. This applies to car insurance, homeowner's and renter's insurance, health insurance, and other private insurance policies. It also covers when a person may want to consult a lawyer or file a complaint, and what deadlines apply for taking action.

terms.name: Homeowner's Insurance
terms.definition: This category covers issues that a homeowner might have with insuring their home, including getting covered by an insurance policy, making claims, dealing with scams or frauds, ending coverage, etc.

terms.name: Renters' Insurance
terms.definition: This category covers a tenant's options to get rental insurance for their home or property they're renting, how to make claims, how to deal with problems or fraud, and how to end coverage.

terms.name: Insurance Scams and Fraud
terms.definition: This category covers options a person might have if they think they may be scammed around an insurance policy, or if they have been accused of insurance fraud. This could be by an insurance company that has deceived the consumer, or if the consumer may be misrepresenting their situation.

terms.name: Life Insurance
terms.definition: This category covers how a person might get, change, use, or end a life insurance policy. It also might cover how a survivor (like a spouse or child) may make claims of the insurance funds after the death.

terms.name: Loans
terms.definition: This category covers issues when a person borrows money, including for school or education (financial aid or student loans), payday loans, and installment purchases. It also covers problems like predatory lending, fraud, or default.

terms.name: Predatory Lending
terms.definition: This category covers situations when a person may be targeted with loan offers that are abusive, fraudulent, or discriminatory.

terms.name: Student Loans and Financial Aid
terms.definition: This category covers issues a person may have when trying to borrow money to pay for school, like around getting financial aid, taking out student loans, paying them back, and dealing with any concerns. This may include how to resolve student loans, understanding aid's conditions, and dealing with possible predatory or fraudulent practices.

terms.name: Payday loans
terms.definition: This category covers options when a person is dealing with short-term, payday loans, which are typically smaller loans with very high fees or interest. This might include issues of falling behind on the loan, overdrafting bank accounts, illegal payday loan companies and practices, or other issues.

terms.name: Understanding the terms of a loan or credit card
terms.definition: This category covers situations when a person is trying to understand the terms of the loan or credit card a person is considering or has taken out, including what obligations a company has under the Truth in Lending Act, and what a person can do if the terms aren't clearly communicated.

terms.name: Canceling (or rescission of) a loan
terms.definition: This category covers consumers' possible right of rescission to cancel a loan or line of credit. This covers when people have this right, how to use it, and what it gives a person.

terms.name: Fees and Finance Charges for a loan
terms.definition: This category covers issues when a person has taken out consumer credit or borrowed money, and is dealing with fees or interest (finance charges) for this borrowing. It includes consumers' rights to know about these charges, how to respond if they seem overly high, or to complain if there has been possible fraud or miscommunication.

terms.name: High interest rates and Usury protections
terms.definition: This category covers issues around high-interest rates on loans and consumer credit, and when a person might be protected by laws that set limits on how much interest can be charged.

terms.name: Having a co-signer taken off a loan
terms.definition: This legal issue covers problems related to removing a co-signer from a loan or credit account, including situations where one borrower wants to be released from responsibility but remains legally liable for the debt. It commonly arises after a relationship ends, financial circumstances change, or the primary borrower falls behind on payments. This category includes disputes where the primary borrower refuses or fails to refinance the loan, despite agreements or expectations that the co-signer would later be removed. It also covers misunderstandings about whether a co-signer can be removed without refinancing, lender requirements for releasing a co-signer, and the impact of late or missed payments on the co-signer’s credit and financial risk. In addition, this issue involves understanding the limited legal options available to a co-signer, such as requesting a co-signer release program (if available), negotiating refinancing, enforcing written agreements, or taking steps to protect credit when removal is not possible. Legal considerations may include contract terms, lender policies, credit reporting consequences, and whether court orders or settlement agreements affect responsibility for the debt. It includes: Requests to remove a co-signer from a loan or lease Refusal by the primary borrower to refinance Credit damage caused by missed or late payments Co-signer release requirements or programs Disputes after breakups, divorce, or separation

terms.name: Taxes
terms.definition: This category covers taxes, including income, sales, property, and other taxes. It covers the obligations and process of calculating and paying taxes, as well as penalties or how to respond to problems. It also covers Earned Income Tax Credits and other social benefit programs.

terms.name: Income Taxes
terms.definition: This category covers how a person's income taxes are calculated and paid, to the federal and state government, based on money that they have made from wages, independent contractor work, royalties, interest, and other sources. It also covers what deductions and benefits might reduce the taxes owed.

terms.name: Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)
terms.definition: This category covers the Earned Income Tax Credit to give low- to moderate-income people with money through a tax credit. This covers who is eligible for an EITC refund, how it is calculated, how family members and income levels affect it, and how to make a claim for EITC.

terms.name: Tax Refunds
terms.definition: Legal issues related to receiving, tracking, correcting, or disputing income tax refunds from federal, state, or local tax authorities. This includes problems with delayed, reduced, missing, or intercepted tax refunds, as well as errors affecting the amount refunded. This issue covers situations where a taxpayer is waiting for a refund that has not arrived, received less than expected, or was offset to pay other debts such as child support, government benefits overpayments, or prior tax liabilities. It also includes errors in tax returns, processing delays, identity verification issues, or problems caused by incorrect bank account information or mailing addresses. It also includes disputes and corrective steps when a refund is affected by fraud, identity theft, or administrative mistakes, such as when a refund is issued to the wrong person or denied because of suspected fraudulent activity. Legal questions may involve how to check refund status, respond to notices from tax authorities, amend a return, request a refund trace, or appeal a refund decision. Rules and timelines vary by jurisdiction and tax authority. Includes: - Delayed, missing, or reduced tax refunds - Errors affecting refund amounts - Refund offsets for debts or obligations - Correcting or amending returns to obtain a refund - Refund issues involving identity theft or fraud - Disputes with tax authorities over refund eligibility or timing

terms.name: Tax disputes and tax court
terms.definition: Disputing a tax assessment, including tax court proceedings and challenging agency decisions.

terms.name: Criminal tax charges
terms.definition: Being investigated or charged with criminal tax evasion or failure to file.

terms.name: International tax issues
terms.definition: Tax issues involving cross-border income, foreign assets, and international reporting.

terms.name: Small Claims lawsuits
terms.definition: This category covers how a person might sue or be sued for a small amount of money. These are called small claim actions, in which the lawsuit covers a small amount of money (usually around $5000 or $10,000 or less), and goes to a special court. It might be for money that one person thinks the other owes them, from a contract, security deposit, accident damages, deceptive business practice, bad check, or land trespass.

terms.name: Going to Small Claims court
terms.definition: This category covers how a person can bring a court case through Small Claims Court, or respond to a small claims lawsuit filed against them.

terms.name: Discrimination against a customer
terms.definition: This category covers situations in which a customer of a business experiences discrimination, either by owners or employees of the business, or other customers. This covers what rights and protections a person has if they face discrimination, and how to use these rights. It also covers what obligations the owners or employees have to deal with the discrimination.

terms.name: Debt and Lending Money
terms.definition: This category is about issues people might have with debts they owe (or other family members owe), dealing with debt collectors, going through a repossession or garnishment process, or filing for bankruptcy. It also covers issues with other people owing you debts, after lending money to them.

terms.name: Debt Collection; Repossession; and Garnishment
terms.definition: This category concerns issues around creditors and debt collectors trying to collect on outstanding loans or debts. This includes taking personal property, wages, liens against real property, freezes on a bank account, or other. This category concerns options, rights, strategies, and exemptions for debtors facing collection.

terms.name: Being a creditor or collecting a debt owed to you
terms.definition: Legal issues for individuals or small businesses collecting money owed to them.

terms.name: Bankruptcy
terms.definition: This issue deals with a person's options regarding filing for bankruptcy, dealing with the procedure of it, and the possible outcomes of it. It concerns issues about who should file for bankruptcy, including around who might be collection-proof. It includes how to file for different kinds of bankruptcy -- Chapter 7, Chapter 11, Chapter 12, or Chapter 13. It also covers exceptions and exemptions, or stays in a bankruptcy.

terms.name: Chapter 7 Bankruptcy for people with limited income
terms.definition: This category concerns the process and consequences of filing for Chapter 7 Bankruptcy, which is an option for individuals whose income is below certain requirements. Chapter 7 bankruptcy liquidates general debts (from credit cards and medical bills) without the need to pay them back. It is typically only available to people with low-income or little/no assets.

terms.name: Chapter 13 Bankruptcy for people with regular income
terms.definition: This category concerns the process and issues of filing for a Chapter 13 'reorganization' bankruptcy for individuals, who have regular income and enough money left over each month to pay back some of their debts (as opposed to those eligible for Chapter 7 'liquidation' bankruptcy). Individuals and sole proprietor companies can apply for Chapter 13 bankruptcy if they meet eligibility requirements. It offers benefits but also requires a payment plan for the debts. It may be used by people who have non-dischargeable debts like for alimony or child support, or for people who have fallen behind on house or car payments and want to catch up on payments and keep the property. It can also be used for debt relief, to lower credit card payments, stop a lawsuit, or prevent wage garnishment.

terms.name: Discharge of Debts in Bankruptcy
terms.definition: This category concerns the options and process of a bankruptcy discharge, when a court orders relieves a person from their obligation to pay a debt. This typically occurs at the end of a Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 bankruptcy hearing. Once a discharge happens, the creditor is prohibited from trying to collect the debt -- though they still may enforce liens attached to secured debts. Not all debts can be discharged in the different kinds of bankruptcy.

terms.name: Exemptions to protect property during bankruptcy
terms.definition: This category concerns options a person might have to claim exemptions during a bankruptcy, which would protect certain property (like home, car, benefits, retirement, licenses, insurance, or tools of trade) from being sold by a trustee during the process. There are federal rules on bankruptcy exemptions, and some states have local exemption systems. This category concerns how to claim certain exemptions, deal with objections to them, and how this determines how much a person will have to pay to creditors.

terms.name: Automatic Stays on creditors during bankruptcy
terms.definition: This category concerns the process of how to get and deal with an automatic stay against most creditors, collection agencies, and government entities when filing for bankruptcy. An automatic stay is a temporary federal injunction, that stops collection efforts against the person. The automatic stay does not extinguish debts, but pauses efforts to collect them. This category concerns limits to the automatic stay, how long it lasts, what happens if creditors violate the order, or how a creditor might remove it.

terms.name: Exceptions to Debt Discharges during Bankruptcy
terms.definition: This category concerns the exceptions of which debts a person might not be able to discharge when filing for bankruptcy. The rules around exceptions will determine which debts a person must still have to pay back, even after going through a Chapter 7, 11, or 13 bankruptcy. This might be based on when the debts were incurred, what kinds of debts they are, or if the person used fraud or false pretenses when borrowing the money.

terms.name: Chapter 11 Bankruptcy for businesses
terms.definition: This category concerns the option and process of filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, which is typically used by larger businesses to reorganize themselves. Chapter 11 bankruptcies allow a company to stay active while repaying creditors and restructuring debts.

terms.name: Chapter 12 Bankruptcy for farmers or fishermen
terms.definition: This category concerns the option and process of filing for Chapter 12 bankruptcy, which is typically used by family farmers or family fishermen to restructure their business. It requires the business to make payments to discharge debts.

terms.name: Being a creditor during bankruptcy
terms.definition: Legal issues for creditors when a debtor files for bankruptcy.

terms.name: Door-to-door Sales - Telemarketing  and Spam
terms.definition: This category covers issues a person may have with a salesperson coming door-to-door trying to sell something, or with telemarketers over phone or text message, or with spam on email. This might include what solicitations are legal, how to opt-out, how to report abuse or fraud, or how to protect oneself against problems.

terms.name: Telemarketers
terms.definition: This category covers consumers' rights and options when dealing with telemarketers over phone or text messages.

terms.name: Door-to-Door Sales
terms.definition: This category covers issues with salespeople who come to homes to sell things, including possible fraud, the ability to stop them from visiting, abuses, and other problems.

terms.name: Spam on Email or Text
terms.definition: This category concerns a person's problem with receiving spam messages over email or text message, including fraud and scams, how to stop unwanted messages, and other issues.

terms.name: Personal Property
terms.definition: Legal issues related to ownership, possession, use, loss, damage, or recovery of personal belongings, including disputes over items that are moved, stored, sold, or disposed of by another person or entity. It covers movable property such as furniture, clothing, vehicles, electronics, and other belongings, but not land or buildings.

terms.name: Abandoned Personal Property
terms.definition: Legal issues related to personal property left behind or treated as abandoned, including rules about notice, storage, retrieval, sale, or disposal of belongings. It often arises after eviction, moving out, incarceration, hospitalization, relationship breakdown, or death, and may involve strict timelines and notice requirements.

terms.name: Civil and Human Rights
terms.definition: This category covers people's fundamental rights, that the government should protect and others should respect. It applies to situations of discrimination, abuse, due process, the first amendment, indigenous rights, and other key rights.

terms.name: Discrimination by Government (Equal Protection)
terms.definition: This category concerns situations in which a person feels that a government body (including at the federal government or state government level) has discriminated against them and caused them harm. This may also be known as an 'equal protection issue', based on the constitutional clause that says the government must treat people equally and fairly.

terms.name: Right to a free lawyer
terms.definition: This category covers a person's possible right to counsel (or a lawyer) that they might have for a specific type of legal matter -- like for a criminal charge, an eviction, or other issue.

terms.name: Disability Rights and Discrimination
terms.definition: This category concerns situations in which someone feels they have been discriminated against based on their disability, or when they may have a right based on their disability. This includes situations around disability rights in education; protecting your employment rights while you have a disability; rights to service dogs and companion animals; voting access; rights to accommodation under the ADA; and otherwise.

terms.name: Disability rights around housing
terms.definition: This category covers what rights a person with a disability may have when it comes to their home, including reasonable accommodation requests they can make from their landlord, defenses they can raise in an eviction, access standards, and dealing with discrimination.

terms.name: Disability rights under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)
terms.definition: This category concerns what rights the ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act) gives to people, who is covered by it, and what obligations it imposes on businesses and people.

terms.name: HIV/AIDS discrimination
terms.definition: This category covers what rights people with HIV/AIDS have, to be protected from discrimination or in getting assistance. It also covers privacy protections for people's health information. This could be in situations at work, health care facilities, schools, daycares, pools, gyms, and other places.

terms.name: Disability discrimination in government programs
terms.definition: This category covers what protections a person with a disability might against discrimination in programs from federal government agencies, groups receiving government assistance, or contractors. This might be under the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and its prohibition on disability-based discrimination in the federal government.

terms.name: Voting Rights
terms.definition: This category concerns what rights people have to vote in federal, state, and local elections -- and how to deal with any problems in voting.

terms.name: Restoring Voting RIghts
